title: No, you are not on Indigenous land
gist: Noah Smith reposts his 2024 essay arguing that land acknowledgements, now ritualized at Democratic Party events, rest on an ethnonationalist theory of collective racial land ownership that delegitimizes the US. He frames the GOP as facing midterm punishment (Trump approval at a term-low -22.4) and proposes instead expanding tribal jurisdiction as a deregulatory tool, citing Vancouver's Squamish-led Sen̓áḵw towers and Tesla showrooms on tribal land.

insights.claim: Noah Smith expects the Republican Party to be punished in the November 2026 midterms for extremism, citing rapidly deteriorating poll support for Trump and the GOP.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A Democratic midterm wave would raise odds of divided government and constrain the administration's policy agenda into 2027-28.
insights.quote: they’re probably going to be punished for it in November; polls show rapidly deteriorating support for both Donald Trump and the GOP

insights.claim: Per Nate Silver as quoted, Trump's approval hit -22.4 in late September 2026, his low for the term and lower than any point in his first term, versus -11.6 at the same point in 2018.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Approval roughly twice as negative as before the 2018 midterm (when Democrats took the House) implies a larger potential swing in 2026.
insights.quote: Trump approval now at -22.4, his low point for the term and now lower than at any point in his first term, even after Jan. 6.

insights.claim: Nate Silver, quoted by Smith, attributes the unusual worsening of Republican midterm polling mostly to gas prices, with AI anxieties possibly also hurting the GOP.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Energy prices and AI-related job anxiety are acting as live political variables, raising pressure for intervention on fuel costs and AI policy before November.
insights.quote: It's gotta be mostly the gas prices, although maybe AI anxieties are also reverberating negatively for the GOP.

insights.claim: Smith argues Democrats, while less extreme than the GOP, have become much more ideologically extreme than in the Obama era, citing opposition to effective immigration enforcement, tolerance of racial discrimination, trans issues and land acknowledgements.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests a Democratic win may not translate into durable political advantage if the party's positioning remains a long-run liability.
insights.locator: Good. Extremism ought to be punished.

insights.claim: Smith contends land acknowledgements do not merely recognize Indigenous people but delegitimize the United States and implicitly advance a theory of collective racial ownership of territory akin to blood-and-soil nationalism.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames a cultural ritual as a substantive ideological signal that could shape voter perceptions of the Democratic Party.
insights.quote: land acknowledgements implicitly advance a theory of collective racial ownership of territory that is morally indistinguishable from the worst blood-and-soil nationalism

insights.claim: Citing Dave Weigel's reporting, land acknowledgements are now part of every major Democratic Party event, a practice absent at the 2016 convention that spread during Obama's second term and Trump's first.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Institutional adoption by the party, not just activist spaces, makes the practice a potential electoral attack vector.
insights.quote: The 2016 Democratic convention did not contain a land acknowledgment.

insights.claim: Smith says land acknowledgements are not a big electoral issue now but represent the creeping rise of anti-American, illiberal ideology on the left that will probably become an electoral liability and departs from the liberal nationalism that made Democrats an effective 20th-century governing party.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Long-run thesis on Democratic coalition durability rather than a near-term electoral driver.
insights.locator: Land acknowledgements are not a big electoral issue

insights.claim: Smith argues all US land was taken by conquest, but so was it before the US, so returning land to the last recorded tribe would merely hand it to the next-most-recent conquerors.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Undercuts the moral basis for restitution claims premised on original ownership.
insights.quote: you would not be returning it to its original occupants; you would simply be handing it to the next-most-recent conquerors

insights.claim: Assigning land to ethnic groups creates an ethnostate in which descendants of immigrants become contingent, perpetual-foreigner citizens; most nations have moved to define citizenship through institutions rather than race.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Positions institutional (civic) nationalism as the stabilizing norm whose erosion would raise political risk globally.
insights.quote: This is the price of ethnonationalism.

insights.claim: Smith argues full 'decolonization' of the US would require dispossessing roughly 330 million people, almost none of Native American descent, which would inevitably involve violence on a colossal scale.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Illustrates why he sees the logic as incompatible with a stable nation-state order.
insights.quote: there are 330 million people here now, and almost none of them descend from Native Americans

insights.claim: If decolonization logic were applied globally, Smith predicts the nation-state order would dissolve into competing irredentist claims backed by genocides and expulsions.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A tail-risk framing: erosion of fixed borders as a norm is a geopolitical destabilizer.
insights.quote: Ten thousand October 7th-style attacks would be followed by ten thousand Gaza-style wars.

insights.claim: Smith argues the world's shift from ethnic cleansing and territorial conquest to fixed borders and institutions should be celebrated and defended, with history remembered to avoid backsliding.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Underlines a pro-status-quo border norm relevant to judging conflicts like Russia's or territorial threats such as toward Greenland.
insights.quote: The most recent of conquests, expulsions, and genocides should be the last to ever happen.
insights.locator: So does this mean we should

themes.theme: Tribal sovereignty as a deregulation tool

insights.claim: Smith argues the better way to honor Native Americans is to give tribal lands autonomy to build housing or industry, and supports Neil Gorsuch's push for the Supreme Court to uphold tribal rights.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Tribal jurisdiction could become a channel for development that bypasses local land-use rules.

insights.claim: In Vancouver, the Squamish Nation is building Sen̓áḵw with developer Westbank: 11 towers and 6,000 apartments on just over 10 acres of reserve land, free of Vancouver's zoning rules, set to be Canada's densest neighbourhood.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete template showing sovereign tribal land can unlock high-density housing supply in constrained, expensive markets.
insights.quote: an 11-tower development that will [put] 6,000 apartments onto just over 10 acres of land in the heart of the city
insights.locator: Vancouver, Canada shows us an example

insights.claim: An even larger development, Jericho Lands, is being planned by a consortium of tribal organizations in Vancouver, and local NIMBYs are objecting that such projects don't fit Indigenous tradition.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Signals a pipeline of tribal-led dense development, with NIMBY opposition shifting to cultural arguments.
insights.locator: An even bigger development called Jericho Lands

insights.claim: Tesla is opening showrooms on tribal lands, including Mohegan Sun (Mohegan Tribe, Connecticut) and Oneida Indian Nation land in New York, to sell directly to consumers and circumvent state dealership-model laws.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Tribal sovereignty offers companies regulatory arbitrage against state laws; direct-sales automakers benefit.

insights.claim: Smith argues American reindustrialization is held back by procedural requirements and local land-use regulation, and tribes using their special legal status to circumvent these barriers could gain jobs and tax revenue while the US gets an end run around NIMBYs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Points to tribal lands as potential sites for factories and industrial projects facing permitting bottlenecks elsewhere.
insights.quote: America would get to execute an end run around the NIMBYs that are holding it back
insights.locator: This sort of thing could lead

insights.claim: Smith cites precedent: in the 1960s Fairchild Semiconductor opened a factory on Navajo land in New Mexico that benefited the economy until an industry downturn and labor dispute ended it in the late 1970s.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that tribal-land industrial siting can work, but remains exposed to industry cycles.
insights.locator: There’s a lot of historical precedent

insights.claim: Smith proposes US cities could, with federal help, transfer parts of their land to tribal jurisdiction, likely yielding dense urban development and satisfying 'land back' desires without endorsing ethnic land rights.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A speculative policy idea that would create new zoning-exempt development zones in US cities.
insights.quote: you’re not living on Indigenous land right now, but you could be in the future — and it might be pretty great
